items.title: M09 — The support desk API, in ASP.NET Core
items.bodyMarkdown:
You have already built this API once. In M02 you built it in Node, and in M01 you
built the React interface that talks to it. Neither of those is changing.

That is the entire point of this mission. `src/SupportDesk.Api/TicketEndpoints.cs`
answers `501 Not Implemented` on every route, and the mission tests describe the
same HTTP contract M02 served: the same paths, the same envelope, the same status
codes, the same cursor pagination over the same total order. When you are done,
the M01 frontend should be able to point at this server and not notice.

What is different is everything underneath. Model binding turns a request into a
typed argument and has its own opinion about what a malformed body is. `string?`
is a compile-time hint, not a promise about what arrived over HTTP, so runtime
validation at the boundary is still yours to write. EF Core will happily give you
whole tracked entities when a projection was what you wanted.

The identity fixture is training scaffolding, not authentication: the dispatcher
arrives in a header and falls back to a fixed fictional one. Do not carry that
pattern anywhere real. Ownership, though, is not scaffolding — it belongs in the
query, and one of the mission tests will tell you if it is not.

Every dispatcher, customer and ticket in this repository is fictional.

PostgreSQL must be reachable. The starter defaults to
`Host=127.0.0.1;Port=5440;Username=postgres` and creates its own database, which
is separate from the DevPractice platform database and from every other
mission's — a training exercise must never be able to touch your learning

```
cp .env.example .env      # adjust only if your server is elsewhere
dotnet restore
dotnet build
```

The SDK is pinned in `global.json` to .NET 10. The first `dotnet restore` on a
cold NuGet cache takes a while; that is the package download, not a hang.

Baseline and mission checks are SEPARATE commands on purpose, so you can always
tell an intentionally incomplete assignment from a broken setup.
baselineChecks: dotnet build — the solution compiles against the pinned .NET 10 SDK
dotnet test --filter Category=Baseline — the app starts, the learning database is reachable and created, the comment foreign key is enforced, and the seed is repeatable
acceptanceCriteria: POST /tickets returns 201 with the stored record and a trimmed title.
POST /tickets rejects an empty or whitespace-only title with 400 and a field-keyed error naming the title, and writes no row.
GET /tickets returns an empty page with a null cursor when there is nothing, rather than an error.
GET /tickets orders by CreatedAt then Id, so two rows sharing a timestamp still have a deterministic order.
Cursor pagination covers every row exactly once across pages, with no duplicates and no gaps.
A caller asking for 500 rows receives at most the bounded page size.
An unknown ticket id returns 404, not 500.
A comment requires an existing ticket the caller owns; otherwise 404 and no row is written.
A comment with an empty body is rejected with 400 and writes nothing.
A dispatcher only sees their own tickets: ownership is enforced in the query.

checklist.label: Baseline passes and Mission fails before I change anything
POST /tickets validates at runtime, returns 201, and writes nothing on a 400
Listing orders by CreatedAt then Id, so the order is total
Cursor paging covers every row exactly once
Page size is clamped regardless of what the caller asks for
Ownership is part of the query, not a filter applied afterwards
I can explain why the M01 frontend needs no change

hints: Start by reading the mission tests as a specification. They were written against the contract M02 already serves, so they tell you the exact shape of every response before you write a line.

Minimal APIs bind the body to your record parameter and inject `SupportDeskContext` from DI. `Results.Created`, `Results.Ok`, `Results.NotFound` and `Results.Json(..., statusCode: ...)` cover every status these tests ask for.

For the page, order by `CreatedAt` then `Id`, take `size + 1` rows, and let the extra row tell you whether another page exists. Decode the cursor into that same pair and compare with `>` on the timestamp OR equal-timestamp-and-greater-id.
items.solutionMarkdown:
The reference solution is one file: `TicketEndpoints.cs`.

Three things are worth naming.

**Validation lives at the boundary.** `request.Title` is typed `string?`, and
that is a compile-time hint. The value arrived over HTTP, so it is checked at
runtime — trimmed, tested for emptiness, bounded in length — before anything is
added to the context. A rejected request returns before `SaveChangesAsync`, which
is why no row appears.

**Ownership is part of the query.** `FirstOrDefaultAsync(t => t.Id == id && t.OwnerId == owner)`
never materialises a row the caller may not see. There is no later filter to
forget and nothing to leak in an error message. This is the same lesson M03
taught in Node, and D08 will make it a policy.

**The cursor and the sort share one total order.** Ordering by a timestamp alone
is ambiguous when two rows share it; adding `Id` makes the order total, and the
keyset comparison uses exactly the same pair. Take one row more than you need and
the extra row answers "is there another page?" without a second count query.
reflectionRubric: I can explain why the M01 React frontend did not have to change when the server language did.
I can say what model binding does for me and what it explicitly does not, and where runtime validation therefore belongs.
I can explain why ordering by CreatedAt alone breaks cursor pagination, and what adding Id fixes.
I can describe where ownership is enforced in my code, and why enforcing it in the UI would not be equivalent.

items.title: M10 — Three defects EF Core will not warn you about
items.bodyMarkdown:
This code runs. It returns plausible JSON. Every baseline check passes. It is
also wrong in three ways, and none of them will ever show up as a stack trace.

That is what makes it worth your afternoon. A crash tells you where to look. This
does not: the list endpoint returns correct comment counts, the detail endpoint
returns the right ticket, and a dispatcher who only ever opens their own tickets
would never notice anything at all.

The mission tests describe the three defects by behaviour rather than by line
number. Two of them are about the SQL EF Core actually sends, which is why the
starter ships a command interceptor: an N+1 and a single joined query return
identical JSON, so the response alone cannot tell you which one you wrote. Read
the captured SQL before you start changing code.

The third defect is the one that matters most, and it is the same class of bug
you repaired in Node in M03. A superficial fix — filtering after loading, or
hiding a control in the interface — will pass neither the test nor review.

Every dispatcher, customer and ticket here is fictional.

The SDK is pinned in `global.json` to .NET 10. The first `dotnet restore` on a

Baseline and mission checks are SEPARATE commands on purpose, so you can always
tell an intentionally incomplete assignment from a broken setup.
baselineChecks: dotnet test --filter Category=Baseline — the app starts, the database is reachable, the owning dispatcher can read their own ticket, and the list returns their tickets with comment counts. All of these pass on the unrepaired starter, which is the point.
acceptanceCriteria: A dispatcher cannot read, list comments on, or rename another dispatcher's ticket: each returns 404.
A response about a foreign ticket leaks nothing about it — no customer name, no owner name.
Listing tickets issues at most one SELECT regardless of how many tickets are returned.
The detail query does not join the comment graph it never returns.
The comments endpoint queries the Comments table directly rather than pulling comments through the ticket graph.
Read-only paths do not track entities.
Comments still come back in order for the legitimate owner: the repair preserves behaviour.

checklist.label: Baseline passes on the unrepaired starter and Mission fails
I read the captured SQL before changing any code
Ownership moved into the query, not into a later filter
A 404 about a foreign ticket leaks nothing about it
The list endpoint issues one SELECT, not one per row
Detail and comments project only what they return
The legitimate owner's behaviour is unchanged

hints: Run the mission tests and read the SQL they print on failure. Two of these defects are visible only in the generated SQL, and one look will tell you more than reading the C# will.

A per-row `await db.Comments.CountAsync(...)` inside a `foreach` is an N+1. EF Core can count in the projection instead: `.Select(t => new TicketSummaryDto(..., t.Comments.Count()))` becomes part of the single query.

For ownership, put `&& t.OwnerId == owner` inside the `FirstOrDefaultAsync` predicate so a foreign row is never materialised. For projection, drop the `Include` on the detail path — `TicketDto` has no comments field — and query `db.Comments` directly with `AsNoTracking()`.
items.solutionMarkdown:
Three repairs, none cosmetic.

**Ownership moved into the query.** `FirstOrDefaultAsync(t => t.Id == id)` became
`... && t.OwnerId == owner`. The foreign row is never loaded, so there is nothing
to leak and no later filter to forget. The rename path gets the same treatment,
which is why the seized-title assertion passes.

**The N+1 became one projected query.** The per-row `CountAsync` is gone; the
count is computed inside the projection, so the database counts and the server
makes one round trip. The JSON is identical — which is precisely why the test
had to assert about SQL rather than about the response.

**Projection replaced graph loading.** The detail endpoint no longer `Include`s
comments it never returns. The comments endpoint queries `Comments` directly and
filters in SQL rather than sorting an in-memory collection. Read paths use
`AsNoTracking()`, because tracking a graph you are about to serialise and discard
buys nothing and costs memory.

The write path deliberately keeps tracking. Tracking is not a mistake; using it
where you only read is.
reflectionRubric: I can explain why every baseline check passed while three real defects were present.
I can describe how I proved the N+1 was gone, and why the JSON response could not have told me.
I can explain why ownership belongs in the query rather than in a filter after loading, or in the interface.
I can say when tracking is the right default and when AsNoTracking is, and what tracking actually costs.

items.title: M11 — Two orders, one last box of lids
items.bodyMarkdown:
`OrderService.PlaceOrderAsync` works. It reads a product, checks the quantity on
hand, decrements it, writes a line and a stock movement, and saves. On a quiet
machine, with one request at a time, it is correct.

The mission puts it under two situations that are not quiet.

The first is a mid-order failure. An order has two lines; the second cannot be
satisfied. The starter has already committed the first line by then, so what is
left behind is an order that half happened — stock decremented for one product,
a movement recorded, and an order row that no customer ever successfully placed.

The second is two orders arriving at once for the last twelve lids. Both read
twelve, both decide eight is fine, and both write. Each write is individually
sensible; together they sell sixteen lids that do not exist. Notice that the
check is not wrong — it is *stale*, and a decision made on stale data must not be
allowed to win silently.

The schema already gives you the tools. `Product.Version` is mapped to
PostgreSQL's `xmin`, so EF Core can tell when a row changed underneath you, and a
check constraint guarantees stock can never go negative no matter what code you
write. Neither of those does anything until `OrderService` uses them.

Every product, order and customer here is fictional.


Baseline and mission checks are SEPARATE commands on purpose, so you can always
tell an intentionally incomplete assignment from a broken setup.
baselineChecks: dotnet test --filter Category=Baseline - the database is reachable and seeded, the seed is repeatable, a single order reduces stock, and the database itself rejects negative stock

dotnet test --filter Category=Baseline - a conflicting edit on a PRODUCT already raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException, which shows the xmin token in the schema works; making the ORDER path handle it is the mission
acceptanceCriteria: A failed line leaves no partial order: no order row, no order lines, no stock movements, and no decremented stock.
Two concurrent orders for the last twelve lids result in exactly one success and one failure.
After those two concurrent orders, stock on hand is four and exactly one order exists.
A successful order still records one line and one stock movement per product and decrements each correctly.

checklist.label: Baseline passes and Mission fails before I change anything
The whole order commits or none of it does
A failed line leaves no order row, no lines, no movements and no decremented stock
A stale decrement is detected rather than overwriting a fresher value
Two concurrent orders for the last twelve lids produce exactly one success
I can explain what the check constraint guarantees that my code does not

hints: Look at where `SaveChangesAsync` is called. Saving inside the loop is what allows a later failure to leave earlier lines committed.

`db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync` gives you an explicit transaction; add every entity first, save once, then commit. If an exception escapes before the commit, the transaction is rolled back and nothing survives.

For the oversell, the concurrency token does the detecting: because `Version` is mapped to `xmin`, a stale UPDATE raises `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` instead of writing. Catch it, discard the stale decision, re-read the product, and decide again — a retry loop of a few attempts is enough.
items.solutionMarkdown:
Two changes, one idea: **a decision made on stale data must not be allowed to
win.**

**One transaction for the whole order.** Every write happens inside
`BeginTransactionAsync`, there is a single `SaveChangesAsync`, and the commit is
the last statement. If a line cannot be satisfied, the exception escapes before
the commit and the transaction rolls back — so there is no half-applied order to
detect or clean up afterwards. The absence of a cleanup path is the feature.

**The stale write is detected, not overwritten.** `QuantityOnHand` is decremented
on a tracked entity whose `xmin` token was read at the start of the attempt. If
another transaction changed that row in between, EF Core raises
`DbUpdateConcurrencyException` rather than writing a number computed from a value
that is no longer true. The retry loop then re-reads and re-decides on fresh data
— which is why one of the two concurrent orders succeeds and the other fails
honestly, instead of both succeeding and overselling.

The check constraint is the backstop, not the mechanism. It guarantees negative
stock can never be persisted even by a code path nobody has written yet. That
pairing — application logic for the expected case, a database constraint for the
case you did not anticipate — is the same one V1 chapter 10 argued for, now with
a concrete failure it prevents.
reflectionRubric: I can explain what the transaction guarantees that careful ordering of statements does not.
I can describe how the xmin concurrency token detects a stale write, and what would happen without it.
I can explain why retrying is safe here, and what would make a retry unsafe.
I can say what the check constraint protects against that my application code does not.

items.title: M12 — The same job, cancelled and rerun, in two languages
items.bodyMarkdown:
You built this job once already, in Node, in M08. This is the same job in C#, and
the mission is only half about the code — the other half is being able to say
what genuinely differs and what merely looks different.

`ReportRunner.RunAsync` processes five source items and writes a row for each.
It works on a first run on a quiet machine. Two things are missing.

It takes a `CancellationToken` and never looks at it. A token nobody checks
cannot stop anything, so a deployment or a timeout has no polite way to interrupt
the run — it either finishes or is killed mid-write. Cancellation in .NET is
cooperative, exactly as an `AbortSignal` is in Node: the type is different, the
discipline is identical.

And a rerun repeats itself. When the first attempt fails on the fourth item,
three rows are already committed. Running it again writes those three a second
time — or would, if the unique index did not stop it, which is worth thinking
about: the constraint turns silent duplication into a loud failure, but a loud
failure is still a failure. Resuming means finishing the remaining work, not
repeating the finished work.

Every business, amount and report row here is fictional.

baselineChecks: dotnet test --filter Category=Baseline — the database is reachable, a clean run writes one row per source item, and the unique index on (JobId, ItemKey) rejects a duplicate row
acceptanceCriteria: A cancelled run stops partway: fewer rows are written than there are source items, and OperationCanceledException escapes.
A rerun after a partial failure completes the job without duplicating the rows already committed, and the attempt count reflects both attempts.
Re-running a job that already succeeded processes nothing and adds no rows.
A clean run still writes exactly one row per source item.

checklist.label: Baseline passes and Mission fails before I change anything
The cancellation token is checked at an item boundary
A rerun finishes the remaining work instead of repeating committed work
Re-running a succeeded job processes nothing
I decided what state a cancelled job should be left in, and can defend it
I can name what genuinely differs from the Node version in M08 and what only looks different

hints: Cancellation is cooperative. `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` inside the loop is the whole mechanism — the question is where in the loop to put it so you stop between units of work rather than half-way through one.

Before processing, ask the database which items this job has already committed: `db.Rows.Where(r => r.JobId == job.Id).Select(r => r.ItemKey)`. Skip those. That single query is what turns a rerun into a resume.

Consider what a cancelled job should look like afterwards. `Failed` is misleading — nothing failed. Leaving it `Queued` with its committed effects intact means the next pass finishes it, which is what makes cancellation safe to use.
items.solutionMarkdown:
Three changes, and the comparison with M08 is the point.

**The token is observed.** `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` at the top of each
item means a shutdown stops the run at an item boundary, never part-way through
one. Node's M08 does the same job with an `AbortSignal` checked in the loop.
Different type, identical discipline — and in both languages, code that never
checks cannot be cancelled politely, no matter how many tokens you thread
through it.

**Committed effects are skipped, not repeated.** The runner reads the `ItemKey`s
already written for this job and processes only the remainder. A rerun after a
partial failure finishes the work; it does not redo it. This is the same
question M07 answered for duplicate order submission in Node, arrived at from a
different direction: there the key was supplied by the caller, here it is derived
from the work itself.

**A cancelled job is not a failed job.** It returns to `Queued` with its
committed effects intact, so the next pass resumes it. Marking it `Failed` would
be a lie about what happened and would need a human to distinguish "we stopped
it" from "it broke".

The unique index on `(JobId, ItemKey)` is the backstop, not the mechanism: it
guarantees a duplicate cannot be persisted even if the skip logic is wrong. That
is the same application-logic-plus-constraint pairing M11 used for stock, and the
reason to have both is that they fail at different moments — one before the
write, one at it.
reflectionRubric: I can explain why cancellation is cooperative and what happens to a token that is never checked.
I can describe how my runner distinguishes work already committed from work still to do, and why that makes a rerun safe.
I can defend the state I leave a cancelled job in, against at least one alternative.
I can name one thing that genuinely differs between the .NET and Node versions of this job, and one thing that only looks different.
